"Wick glass is not lamp wick," she said before hello. "People hear wick and think flame. No flame. If you put flame near charge glass, I throw you in lake. Not literally because paperwork, but spiritually yes."

"Strong orientation."

"You sort. You do not polish, scrape, re-seat, warm, bend, charge, compare brightness by eye, or decide what a weird one means."

"Question bin."

"Question tray. Bin sounds like we don't care. We care aggressively."

**DULL RETURN**

**QUESTION**

Check for obvious chip, cloud spread, hairline fracture, darkened anchor end.

Do not grade brightness.

Do not decide serviceability.

"Why sort clear and dull if I don't grade?"

Mera pointed at card marks.

"Because crew already marked behavior before removal. You match marked condition to physical strip. Clear-return card goes clear-return tray unless physical damage makes question. Dull-return card goes dull-return tray unless mismatch makes question."

"Exactly."

"No."

Good.

"Brightness depends bowl, wick, charge, moisture, angle, distance, contamination, whether some idiot cleaned outer glass with fish oil, and probably moods of dead ancestors."

"Last one measured?"

"Extensively."

"Useful conclusion then?"

"Pilots don't use brightness as number. They use whether expected shore glow is present, absent, distorted, doubled, or displaced relative to route markers."

There.

"Comparative navigation."

"Yes."

"Not fog measurement."

"Yes."

I sorted faster once system settled.

Not too fast.

Careful-hands job paid for not being interesting.

A young technician at next table, **Risa Pell**, was fitting a wick strip into bronze fork.

Pell.

Names everywhere.

She caught me looking.

"You want one?"

"Can't afford lunch emotionally."

"Good. Retired wick glass is mostly decorative unless you own bowl housing."

"Mostly?"

"People make jewelry. Bad jewelry."

"Dangerous?"

"Usually just ugly."

Reassuring.

A runner came in from South Tower.

"Two bowl showing double edge."

Mera stopped talking.

"In fog?"

"Lower bank rolling in. Pilot Three reported split glow from west approach."

Mera looked to technician table.

"Risa. Bowl Two return set from yesterday?"

"Bench three."

They moved.

I did not.

Sort.

Runner waited.

Mera checked yesterday's returned wick set against service card.

One strip had been marked dull but no fracture.

Risa said, "Could be bowl suspension."

Mera: "Could be outer skin condensation. Could be second reflection off wet causeway. Could be wick seat. We don't get to pick favorite."

Runner asked, "Do we close west approach?"

Mera said, "Keeper decides navigation status. Tell tower we have no bench cause yet. Ask if double edge persists after bowl shield reset."

Runner left.

Again.

People with actual authority did authority.

I matched cards.

Fifteen more.

Question strip with hairline crack.

Question strip whose stamped number didn't match card.

Question card marked clear but glass physically smoky at one edge.

Mera checked mismatch.

"Wrong return pouch."

She did not silently fix.

Logged transfer.

Systems hate undocumented helpful people.

High Shelf again.

Regional religion.

Second runner came.

"Shield reset fixed split. West approach remains open."

Mera nodded.

"Then likely external reflection or shield seat. Bowl Two stays in service pending afternoon physical check."

"Not wick?"

"Not proven wick."

Good.

No dramatic failure.

No ferry disaster.

Just navigation system producing ambiguous symptom and people narrowing it.

I finished half shift.

Mera counted trays.

"Forty-eight matched. Six question."

"Is that good?"

"It's forty-eight matched and six question."

Perfect.

She paid three copper.

Twelve to fifteen.

Five above floor.

Breathing room.

Small.

Real.

I did not immediately buy ferry ticket.

Growth.

Outside, fog had moved across lower lake in pale sheets.

South Tower bowl glowed softly.

Now that I knew what it wasn't, it looked more useful.

Not a beacon saying HERE.

A reference saying expected shore glow currently behaves like this.

Pilots built rest from experience.

Same as bottom-change plates.

Same as half the tools I liked.

No absolutes.

Just better questions.

I went to landing board.

Routes unchanged except one new note.

**NORTH SHORE / REEDMARK / 3C / AFTERNOON FOG HOLD POSSIBLE**

**EAST CROSSING / LAKEWARD / 4C / NOON WINDOW CLOSED / NEXT REVIEW TOMORROW**

**LOWER LAKE / TOLLEN / 2C / DEPART SECOND RING**

Too late for Tollen today.

Good.

Forced patience.

I asked ticket clerk what each place actually was.

"Reedmark?"

"North-shore reed-cutting town. Ferry yards, marsh road, uplake carts."

"Lakeward?"

"East-side market town. Bigger. Cross-lake freight, glass works, road east toward orchard country."

"Tollen?"

"Lower lake fish town. Cheap beds. South road reconnects valley routes."

There.

Different choices.

Reedmark opened north shore and marsh road.

Lakeward opened glass works and orchard country east.

Tollen looped lower lake and south roads.

Lakeward strongest expansion.

Also four copper.

At fifteen, paying four leaves eleven.

Then lodging could hit ten exactly.

Too thin.

Could work tomorrow again.

But not same sort job by default.

Could maybe earn another small job.

Or take Reedmark three, leave twelve.

Still one-copper lodging leaves eleven.

Thin but better.

Or stay South Larken another day and build buffer.

This was not fake choice.

I sat by public quay with bowl tower behind me.

Freshwater gull equivalent? Small black lake birds fought over peel.

One won.

Capitalism but feathers.

Caro Olt passed carrying repaired net panel.

"Still here."

"Financially."

"Where going?"

"Maybe east. Maybe north."

"East costs more."

"I noticed."

"North smells worse."

"Useful metric."

"Reedmark marsh mud gets in boots."

He looked at crutches.

"Or... whatever you've got."

"Currently one boot and two sticks."

"Then mud gets in stick ends. Worse."

Good point.

"Lakeward?"

"Too many people. Glass workers think every piece of clear junk deserves ceremony. Market decent."

"Road beyond?"

"Orchards east. Hill towns after. Never went."

"Why not?"

"Lake here."

Simple.

His world did not need expansion.

Mine apparently did.

That thought bothered me slightly.

Not because wrong.

Because easy to turn movement into virtue.

Staying wasn't failure.

Going wasn't courage automatically.

I was traveling because I wanted to.

Important.

At South Landing, a ferry crew began unloading baskets of long silver fish.

One basket had glass tag with pale green thread.

Another amber.

I asked worker after load clear.

"Temperature?"

"Freshness interval."

"Meaning?"

"Tag changes after enough warm exposure. Not clock."

Of course.

"Resettable?"

"Some. These no. Cheap freight tags."

"Accurate?"

Worker shrugged.

"Accurate enough buyer rejects amber if contract says green."

Economic instrument.

Not scientific absolute.

Interesting.

Artifact market everywhere, just embedded in labor.

I did not ask price.

Wallet thanked me.

Afternoon I stayed local.

Actual life.

Bought stew with bits.

Watched fog bank cross without drama.

Helped Net House keeper move three empty stools because I was there and had hands? Crutches complicate. Could carry one stool one-handed awkwardly. Better not.

I sharpened pencil.

Wild adventure.

Later, public tower keeper gave short explanation to two apprentice pilots.

I listened from public side.

Expected pattern:

South Bowl visible first on west approach.

Causeway bowl second.

If both visible but spacing looks wrong, suspect lateral drift or reflection.

If one absent, do not infer bowl failure immediately because fog wall can hide local reference.

Pilots compare with route memory and bottom-change plates.

Multiple weak instruments together create stronger navigation.

That was beautiful.

Not because magic.

Because system.

I wrote it down:

**Lake navigation does not trust one instrument. Bowl gives shore relation. Bottom plate gives bottom-change relation. Pilot gives route memory. Fog posts constrain road approach. None sufficient alone.**

Then underlined:

**Useful systems overlap imperfect evidence.**

Probably true beyond boats.

Could apply to human conflict too.

Dangerous thought.

I left it.

Evening board updated:

**REEDMARK NORTH SHORE / MORNING WINDOW LIKELY / 3C**

**LAKEWARD EAST / MORNING REVIEW / 4C / CROSS-LAKE FOG POSSIBLE**

No need choose tonight.

Net House second night still 1c.

I paid.

Fifteen to fourteen.

Four above floor.

Same damn number.

But this time I had not moved.

That mattered.

I had spent one copper to learn place instead of three or four to leave it.

Maybe good.

Maybe just slower capitalism.

I sent home note next morning? Could send tonight. Enough time since previous note departed Mere Ridge yesterday. Fine.

**South Larken. Stayed another night. Earned 3c sorting returned wick glass at Fog Bowl House. Fog bowls are shore-reference tools, not fog meters or lamps. South approach had a double-glow report today; shield reset cleared it, no proven wick failure. Cash 14c, Vale 23c after second Net House night. Ten floor intact. No onward ticket yet. - Greg**

Then:

**Lakeward east is 4c. Reedmark north is 3c. I am attempting the radical experiment of not buying transportation immediately after earning money.**

Postage bits.

Trial leg rested all day.

Good.

Lot 67 packed.

Good.

Magic 138 still enough.

Good.

Before bed, fog thickened enough South Bowl disappeared from Net House window.

Then pale glow returned ten breaths later through different patch.

Not signal failure.

Fog geometry.

I understood that now.

Tiny thing.

Still satisfying.

Lamplighter was wrong technically.

No lamps.

But I had spent half day sorting pieces that made shore glow in fog.

Close enough for chapter title.

Tomorrow I could go north.

Or east.

Or work again.

For once, I had enough money to choose badly without immediately becoming broke.

Luxury.
# CHAPTER 458

## THE WAYFINDER

Lakeward ferry posted green at first ring.

That was inconvenient.

I had spent last night hoping weather would make decision for me.

Very mature.

South Larken board:

**LAKEWARD EAST / 4C / CLEAR WINDOW / LOAD CALL FIRST-AND-HALF**

Cash fourteen.

Ten-copper floor.

Four copper fare.

Which would leave exactly ten.

Then lodging would require violating my own rule before I had even found bed.

No.

Reedmark north remained three copper.

Tollen two.

Crown Vale was now west behind ridge.

All sensible.

Lakeward still pulled hardest.

Glass works.

Orchard road.

East country.

Different.

I stared at board until clerk said, "You buying or courting it?"

"Financially incompatible relationship."

"Then move."

Fair.

One small job had appeared below route board.

**LANDING THREE / DEPARTURE TOKEN CHECK / 1C / ONE BELL / SEATED**

Not enough to be interesting.

Exactly enough to be useful.

I took it.

No heroic labor.

No half-day delay.

One bell at a little table beside boarding lane.

Job was stupidly simple.

Passenger handed token.

I matched stamped route notch to clerk sheet.

Green basket Lakeward.

Blue Reedmark.

Yellow Tollen.

Wrong basket went back to clerk.

No fare disputes.

No identity judgments.

No upgrades.

Just stop people getting onto wrong boats before wrong boat became expensive geography.

I caught three.

Woman with Tollen token in Lakeward line.

Man with yesterday's void Reedmark chit.

One child carrying mother's token while mother held child's.

That one technically would have solved itself.

Still counted.

One copper.

Fourteen to fifteen.

Now Lakeward fare left eleven.

One-copper floor bed would leave ten.

Thin.

But not fake.

I bought east crossing.

Fifteen to eleven.

No joy.

A ferry ticket should feel like possibility.

Mine felt like subtraction.

Good.

Trial leg stayed wrapped.

It had rested yesterday, but wet deck, cross-lake fog possibility, and unknown landing surface made crutches correct.

I boarded **Glass Heron** through lower ramp.

Broader than lower-lake boats.

Two shallow hulls joined under a wide deck? No. Not twin hulls. One broad hull with side outriggers? Keep simple.

Broad flat-bellied hull, low cabin, high reed-slat wind screens.

At bow, two bottom-change plates hung folded upward for open water.

Fog bowl mounted aft under hood.

Pilot **Rian Kett**.

Deck crew three.

Passengers maybe twenty.

Freight mostly orchard crates, glass cullet sacks, lamp oil, seed baskets.

I found bench against wind screen.

No one knew me.

Still nice.

Then somebody said, "Peg-Leg Greg?"

Damn it.

I looked.

Teenage boy with apple crate.

"No."

He grinned.

"My aunt came through High Shelf two days ago. Said there was tall one-legged man with trial limb heading lake road."

"That's circumstantial."

"She said he talks annoying."

"Could be anybody."

He laughed.

Nickname had beaten mail somehow.

Fine.

"I don't even have peg."

"Yet."

Kett Arlo's disease spreading by trade routes.

Boy's name **Perrin Sol**.

Orchard apprentice from east side.

He was returning with rootstock.

"Lakeward?" I asked.

"Then east road."

"How far?"

"Home? Half day cart if road dry."

"Where?"

"Morrow Orchard."

New place.

"Big?"

"Enough."

Good answer.

Glass Heron left South Landing.

Shore fog was lifting, but lake still held gray bands farther east.

Open water changed sound.

Sea ferries had constant salt chop and long swell memory.

Larken had shorter motion.

Wind-made.

Patchy.

Surface dark in one direction, silver in another.

Caro's line returned.

Lake wind lies.

Pilot Rian watched water like it was handwriting.

Bottom plates stayed up.

Fog bowl aft dark.

No need.

For first half bell nobody talked much.

Then older woman across aisle started telling story to two children.

Not performance.

Something they had clearly heard before and wanted again.

"Tell the cup one."

"You know cup one."

"Tell it."

She sighed like storyteller defeated by market demand.

"Fine."

I listened because sitting did not require moral justification.

Story was called **The Woman Who Returned the Water**.

Not ancient-god proclamation.

A woman named **Iria** lived in orchard country during a dry year.

Spring above orchards thinned.

People fought over channels.

Upper farms closed gates.

Lower farms accused them of theft.

Village measurers argued whether spring itself was failing or water was being held.

Iria's grandmother told her there was older water path before the cut road.

Not road exactly.

Sequence of places.

Lakeward shore.

White Reed.

Sleeping Stone.

Three Sisters Hollow.

Mirror Spring.

Iria carried a plain cup of lake water uphill.

At each place she poured some out.

Not because lake water magically fed spring.

Because the path marked where water changed.

At White Reed, soil stayed wet though channel was dry.

At Sleeping Stone, moss lived on downhill face.

At Three Sisters, one hollow still held frogs.

At Mirror Spring, she found spring mouth blocked by fallen root and stone after storm.

She cleared enough for water to move.

Then carried a black spring pebble back down and placed it in lake.

Children asked why.

Old woman said, "Because story says water remembers road both ways."

One child said, "Rocks don't remember."

"Then remember for rock."

Good.

That line landed.

I expected ending.

Didn't get one.

Woman continued.

On way home Iria met three farmers arguing at lower gate.

They wanted to know who caused dry channels.

She told them storm blocked spring.

Upper farmer said that proved he had not stolen.

Lower farmer said upper still closed too much gate.

Third said everybody would lie again next drought.

So they set marker stones at channels and agreed each family had to walk spring path once before accusing another.

Children hated administrative ending.

"That's boring."

"That's why you still have apples."

Excellent.

Perrin beside me had gone quiet.

"Your orchard?" I asked softly.

He looked.

"What?"

"Morrow. Is that in story country?"

His expression changed.

Not dramatic.

More careful.

"Yeah."

"Mirror Spring real?"

"Depends which old person you ask."

"That's not answer."

"There's spring called Mirror. Path isn't used now. Cut road goes around north shoulder."

I looked back toward storyteller.

She was correcting child pronunciation of Three Sisters place-name.

"Still water problem?"

Perrin stared at crate.

"Not like story."

There.

Somebody wanted something badly maybe.

"What's like story?"

"Nothing."

Then, after a while:

"East channels are low."

"Drought?"

"Maybe."

"Upper gates?"

"Maybe."

"Spring?"

"Maybe."

"You have excellent evidence."

"I know."

He sounded irritated.

Not at me exactly.

Good.

"Why were you west buying rootstock if channels low?"

"Because my mother already paid."

Human answer.

"And because if water comes back, we need it."

"If?"

He rubbed crate edge.

"District reader says wait three days. Water office wants another channel measure. Upper orchards say lake fog changed recharge. Lower orchards say upper gates are cheating. My grandfather says somebody needs to walk old path."

"And what do you say?"

"I say grandfather can't walk it."

There.

Quest arrived quietly.

Not mine.

Somebody else's.

"You?"

"I have work."

"That's convincing."

He glared.

"You don't know my family."

"Correct."

I shut up.

Good.

Glass Heron crossed gray band.

Fog bowl aft lit pale.

Crew did not panic.

Pilot adjusted east by maybe small angle.

A deckhand called marker number.

Bottom-change plates lowered as shore shelf approached.

Water under us darkened green over weed beds.

One plate gave faint line.

Pilot shifted north.

Layered imperfect evidence.

Worked.

Lakeward emerged through fog in pieces.

First glass towers.

Not towers like castle.

Tall kiln chimneys with pale exhaust.

Then shoreline cranes.

Then long low buildings with roofs of blue-gray tile.

Orchard carts everywhere.

Apples, pears, long yellow fruit I didn't know.

Freshwater reeds bundled by docks.

East side smelled like wet wood and hot glass.

No salt.

Still strange.

We docked.

Perrin lifted rootstock crate.

Too heavy for him alone.

Deckhand helped.

I did not volunteer with crutches on wet ramp.

Growth.

At landing square, story woman disappeared into market.

Perrin waited near road board.

I looked too.

**ORCHARD ROAD / MORROW / 2C CART / SECOND BELL**

**GLASS ROAD / EAST WORKS / 1C CART**

**NORTH SHORE / REEDMARK / 3C FERRY**

**LOWER LAKE / TOLLEN / 2C**

Morrow Orchard.

Two copper.

I had eleven.

Could not pay and preserve floor.

Not without work.

Again.

But now there was reason beyond novelty.

Not obligation yet.

Reason.

Perrin saw me read Morrow line.

"Don't."

"Don't what?"

"Make face like you're thinking."

"My face does that."

"Grandfather will hire anybody who listens to story."

"That's poor hiring practice."

"Exactly."

I almost laughed.

"Hire for what?"

"Walk."

"Old path?"

"He wants somebody to go from White Reed to Mirror Spring and mark wet signs before district crew finishes arguing."

"Why not you?"

He got angry this time.

"Because I have two younger sisters, mother, six rows already stressed, and I am apprentice under east graft house. If I disappear three days because grandfather wants story walk, we lose more than water."

There.

No clean answer.

"How long is path?"

"Nobody knows now."

"That's bad."

"Yes."

"Passable?"

"Grandfather says yes."

"That is not evidence."

"I know."

He was learning my language fast.

"District maps?"

"Old path crosses landslide cut beyond Three Sisters. New road goes around."

"So grandfather wants stranger with one leg to inspect abandoned footpath."

Perrin looked at crutches.

"I said hiring practice bad."

Fair.

I should walk away.

Actually I should crutch away.

Cash eleven.

Ten floor.

No room.

Unknown path.

Unknown lodging.

Unknown work.

Borrowed trial leg.

No reason to inherit orchard family's problem.

Then Perrin said:

"He pays eight copper if somebody reaches Mirror Spring and comes back with route notes. Twelve if they also bring sealed spring sample to district office."

Oh.

Real money.

Not miraculous.

Several days risk for eight to twelve.

Could matter.

Could fund road.

Could maybe feed leg money indirectly.

Could also cost more than paid.

"Why twelve for sample?"

"District office wants it. Grandfather says if we're walking anyway, bring sample."

"Who provides bottle?"

"District."

"Authority?"

"Sample only. No gate authority."

Good.

"Why hasn't district sent somebody?"

"They will. Eventually."

"How eventually?"

"Three days maybe. Five if reader team stays north channels."

"And orchard?"

"Lower rows start losing fruit if channels stay this low another two or three days."

There.

Clock.

Not world ending.

Fruit.

Work.

Family.

Money.

Old story path.

Modern measurement delay.

Somebody needed something.

I hated how well it fit.

"Grandfather name?"

"Teren Sol."

"Morrow Orchard?"

"Yes."

"Does he know you are recruiting one-legged strangers at ferry docks?"

"No."

"Excellent."

"He will like you."

"That worries me."

I still did not agree.

Important.

First lodging.

Lakeward cheap board showed:

**GLASS YARD FLOOR / 1C / WORKERS + TRAVELERS**

I paid.

Eleven to ten.

Exactly floor.

No discretionary copper.

There.

Adventure officially required income.

I put pack at Glass Yard floor.

Dry stable stone.

Trial limb had rested all day? No wear today. Could use later, but not necessary. Keep rest.

Then I went to district water office.

Not because quest accepted.

Because check claims before becoming idiot.

Office clerk **Aven Rusk** found Morrow notice after some searching.

"Low east channels."

"How low?"

"Enough for watch, not emergency."

"Mirror Spring sample requested?"

"Requested if field team reaches source."

"Can private person bring one?"

"Sealed district bottle, witness mark at fill, accepted as supplemental. Not authoritative source reading by itself."

Good.

"Old path?"

Aven made face.

"Story path."

"Real?"

"Parts."

"Passable?"

"Depends what you call path."

"Accessible with crutches?"

She looked at me properly.

"I would not promise that."

Finally.

"Landslide?"

"Three Sisters north shoulder. New road bypasses. Old footpath may cross lower bench. We do not maintain it."

"Any map?"

"Public archive sketch. No current condition."

She pulled thin sheet.

White Reed.

Sleeping Stone.

Three Sisters Hollow.

Mirror Spring.

Same sequence.

Story was map memory.

Not exact map.

But map.

Hawaiian-story nudge in world's own grammar: story holds geography, practical observation, social rule.

I copied route names.

"Bottle?"

"We don't issue unless someone signs supplemental sample chain."

"Can I see form?"

She handed.

Simple enough.

Collector name.

Route.

Fill point.

Witness if available.

Seal number.

Observed conditions.

No claim of source flow rate.

No claim of cause.

Good.

"Fee?"

"Deposit one copper on bottle. Refunded when returned intact, sample or empty."

I had zero discretionary.

Of course.

"Can orchard post deposit?"

"Yes."

Interesting.

I returned form.

"Not signing yet."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Because people sign before asking where Mirror Spring is."

"I asked."

"That's why good."

I left.

Perrin was waiting by market fountain.

"You went office."

"I enjoy ruining stories with paperwork."

"Grandfather is at Morrow tomorrow morning."

"I have no money for cart."

"He'll pay cart if he wants you."

"That sounds suspiciously like free fare."

"It's employment travel."

Damn technically legitimate economics.

"I haven't accepted."

"I know."

He stopped pushing.

Good.

"Can he come here?"

"He won't leave rows."

Human problem again.

"Then I either spend work time going to him or don't."

"Yes."

"Any work here tomorrow early?"

"Glass yard always has something."

Not guarantee.

I went work board.

**GLASS RETURN CRATE PAD / 2C / FIRST RING / SEATED OK**

There.

Not exciting.

But enough to restore floor margin before deciding.

I marked it mentally.

No claim yet.

At Glass Yard floor, kiln glow painted ceiling orange through high windows.

I opened notebook.

Wrote:

**Potential actual job: Morrow Orchard, Teren Sol. Old story route White Reed -> Sleeping Stone -> Three Sisters -> Mirror Spring. 8c route notes; 12c with sealed supplemental spring sample. District confirms low east channels + sample accepted as supplemental only. Old path unmaintained; current accessibility unknown; landslide near Three Sisters. Lower rows may lose fruit in 2-3 days.**

Then:

**This is somebody else's problem.**

I stared.

Added:

**Which is usually how adventure starts.**

Annoying.

No quest accepted.

Not yet.

But for first time since leaving Carrow, tomorrow had something more specific than next town.

A person.

A place.

A path.

A reason to reach end and come back.

That felt different.

Wayfinder.

Not because I knew way.

Because story did.

Maybe.
# CHAPTER 459

## THE CONTRACTOR

Adventure started with crate padding.

Naturally.

Lakeward Glass Yard first ring smelled like wet wood, ash, and somebody else's expensive mistake.

I had ten copper.

Exactly ten.

Floor had stopped being policy and become current account balance.

Twenty-three Vale remained separate.

Leg money remained leg money.

Mirror Spring remained a sentence in notebook.

Before I let sentence become several days of bad terrain, I wanted two things.

Money.

Then Teren Sol's actual mouth.

Not Perrin's summary of it.

Glass Return Crate Pad paid two copper for one ring.

I took it.

Supervisor **Hala Renn** pointed at bench.

"Returned crates only. Pull old reed pad. Check frame for obvious split. New pad goes corners and base. If frame split, red chalk and stop. You are not a cratewright."

"I am collecting professions I am not."

"Good. Collect quietly."

Trial leg had rested.

Dry bench floor.

But I was leaving town after if job existed.

Unknown route.

Save skin.

Crutches.

I sat.

Crate padding was satisfying in way repetitive work sometimes became when endpoint obvious.

Old reed out.

Frame look.

No split.

New reed in.

Tie.

Stack.

Second crate had corner separation.

Red chalk.

Stop.

Third smelled like vinegar.

"Problem?" I asked.

Hala sniffed.

"Cleaning return. Fine."

Fourth had glass dust under base seam.

Question.

She swept sample onto black card.

"Old break residue. Crate cleared yesterday. Pad replacement only."

Fine.

No mystery.

No quest in crate.

Good.

At end of ring she counted two copper.

Ten to twelve.

I liked twelve better.

Still thin.

But floor had breathing room.

I found Perrin at east cart stand carrying graft knives in wrapped roll and arguing with man about axle space.

Not angrily.

Persistently.

"It's one roll."

"One roll becomes twelve rolls when everybody says one roll."

"Mine actually is one."

"That's what makes it dangerous."

Perrin saw me.

"You came."

"I came to ask your grandfather whether you invented his money."

"I rounded."

"Up?"

"No."

Interesting.

Cart master found knife roll space under bench for one bit.

Perrin paid.

"Morrow cart?" I asked.

"Second ring."

"Fare?"

"Two copper. Grandfather covers if you're coming about spring."

"He said that?"

"He said bring anyone willing to listen before talking."

"That's not same sentence."

Perrin exhaled.

"No. It isn't."

Good.

"Then I talk first."

"Fine."

I paid nothing.

We waited for cart.

Perrin did not fill silence well.

He tried anyway.

"The story isn't exactly how my grandfather tells it."

"Already encouraging."

"He says Iria didn't clear the spring."

There.

"What does he say?"

"She found where water went."

"Different."

"Yes."

"Where did it go?"

"Depends which time he tells it."

Better.

"And you want me to work for this man."

"I want somebody to go before lower pears drop."

That was honest.

"Why you?"

"Because my mother won't leave rows. Grandfather's knee won't take Three Sisters. My sisters are eleven and eight. Graft house already gave me yesterday afternoon because ferry was late. If I disappear three days, I lose placement."

"Could lose fruit instead."

"Yes."

No clean answer.

Cart arrived.

Morrow Orchard cart was flat farm wagon with canvas half roof and bins of empty produce trays going east.

Driver **Nemi Cross** checked Perrin's pass.

Perrin pointed at me.

"Possible spring hire."

Nemi said, "Possible doesn't ride account."

Correct.

Perrin opened mouth.

I said, "I'll pay two. If Teren hires me and travel is covered, he reimburses. If not, my trip."

Ten-floor problem.

Twelve to ten.

Exactly floor again.

But this was deliberate information cost, not casual spending.

Was that rational?

Maybe.

Could have demanded Teren come Lakeward.

But orchard clock mattered.

And I wanted to see channels.

Paid two.

Twelve to ten.

Adventure apparently hated liquidity.

Cart east.

Lakeward glass roofs receded.

Road climbed gently through orchards.

Rows first sparse.

Then continuous.

Pear-like trees? Avoid Earth exact maybe fruit types can be pears established by Perrin line. Fine.

Some wet.

Some barely.

Not one irrigation system.

Many linked ones.

Second less.

Not dry.

Low.

Did not touch.

"Measured?"

"Not by me."

Good correction.

"Who?"

"Gate keeper chalk board."

Cluster of family holdings around packing shed, graft house, drying yard, and shared lower channel.

Morrow apparently district name older than current families.

Teren Sol sat under shade roof repairing basket handles.

Late sixties maybe.

Broad shoulders reduced by age rather than erased.

Left knee wrapped.

He looked at my crutches.

Then at Perrin.

Perrin stiffened.

I liked Teren less immediately.

Useful.

"To find out what you're actually hiring for before I decide whether your bad knee and my missing foot should negotiate terrain by proxy."

Perrin looked at ground.

Teren barked laugh.

Not warm.

But real.

I sat.

He did not know Peg-Leg Greg.

Excellent.

"Perrin says eight for route notes, twelve with sealed spring sample."

"Eight if you reach source and return useful notes. Twelve with district bottle filled and sealed correctly."

Good.

"When your knee worked?"

Pause.

"Yes."

There.

"Landslide?"

"Three if slow."

"Unknown if blocked."

"Yes."

Perrin coughed into hand.

Teren stared.

Then said, "Three days food."

Good.

Not victory.

Basic planning.

"Turnaround condition?"

"What?"

"When do I stop trying and come back?"

"If path gone."

"Define gone."

"You enjoy this?"

"More than falling."

He rubbed wrapped knee.

"If Three Sisters lower bench is cut through, don't climb north face. Old upper track crosses loose shelf."

Specific.

"Current?"

"Don't know."

"Weather?"

Perrin answered. "Dry two days. Ridge fog mornings. No rain posted."

Teren nodded.

"Overhang. Dry unless east wind."

"People on route?"

Now adventure.

"They are coming."

"Then why me?"

Teren leaned forward.

"Because three days is three days. Because lower fruit doesn't care whose seal is on paper. Because if source is running strong, I want to know before Halden families close another gate and call it conservation. Because if source is weak, I want Perrin's mother to stop accusing people who may not be stealing anything."

There.

Human problem.

"And because you want old path proven."

His eyes narrowed.

Perrin had warned me.

"I want people to remember there was a path before district road decided water begins where measuring box is."

"That's different job."

"Same mountain."

"Not same job."

Teren got angry quietly.

"You think because office draws new line the old one stops carrying water?"

"No. I think if you pay me to inspect source, I need to know whether you're paying for evidence or vindication."

Silence.

Perrin finally said, "Grandfather."

Teren looked at him.

Perrin kept going.

Messier now.

"This is what I meant. You keep saying walk it, walk it, walk it like if somebody puts feet on every old stone then everyone has to admit you were right about closing the lower marker council, and that's not what we need right now. We need to know if water is there. We need to know if something happened above Three Sisters. Mom doesn't care if the old path gets a plaque. She cares if Row Four drops fruit."

Teren's face changed.

Not defeated.

Hurt.

Good.

Somebody else's story.

Teren said, "Your mother learned that channel on my back."

"I know."

"You learned White Reed because I took you."

"I know."

"Then don't talk like memory is decoration."

"I'm not. I'm saying pears are dying while you argue about memory."

No sarcasm academy.

No clean winner.

I waited.

Eventually Teren looked at me.

"Evidence," he said.

"Route notes too?"

"Yes."

"Separate sections."

He frowned.

"What?"

"One page: route condition. One page: water observations. No mixing `old marker missing` with `upper family stole water`."

"Fine."

"Sample supplemental only."

"Fine."

"I do not accuse Halden families for you."

"Fine."

"I do not prove story."

Longer pause.

"Fine."

Perrin exhaled.

I wasn't done.

"Pay. Twelve with valid sealed sample. Eight if source reached and route notes returned but sample invalid or impossible. Four if I reach Three Sisters and route beyond is unsafe under agreed turnaround, with notes showing where and why."

Teren said, "Four for failing?"

"Four for useful route information that prevents next person from discovering same failure."

He hated it.

Thought.

"Three."

"Four."

"Three and your cart fare back."

"Four and cart fare already paid reimbursed now if hired."

Perrin whispered, "He's going to die bargaining before trail."

Teren ignored him.

"Four. Fare reimbursed."

"Good."

Contract.

Not paper yet.

We went packing shed office.

Morrow clerk wrote terms.

**MIRROR SPRING SUPPLEMENTAL WALK**

Employer: Morrow lower-channel cooperative, signed Teren Sol under emergency field-observation allowance? Need not invent legal detail too much. Better private cooperative job with district sample form separate.

Terms:

- route: Morrow -> White Reed -> Sleeping Stone -> Three Sisters -> Mirror Spring where safely passable;
- return route notes + water observations;
- 12c if valid district supplemental source sample returned with completed seal form;
- 8c if source reached and useful route notes returned but valid sample cannot be completed;
- 4c if Three Sisters reached and continuation judged unsafe under specified conditions, with useful route notes;
- Lakeward->Morrow 2c fare reimbursed upon hire;
- three days food + blanket roll supplied;
- district bottle deposit supplied by employer;
- no authority to alter gates, clear source, move markers, enter closed private channels, or represent district;
- Greg may turn back earlier for injury, weather, route loss, or equipment failure, but sub-Three-Sisters return has no guaranteed field pay beyond reimbursement/supplies consumed in good faith.

Good.

Teren paid my two copper reimbursement.

Ten to twelve.

Buffer restored.

He did not advance wages.

Fair.

"Bottle tomorrow," Perrin said. "District office runner comes Morrow first ring."

"Departure after?"

Teren said, "White Reed by midday if road dry."

"Road?"

"Farm track first part. Old path starts after keeper house."

"Guide?"

"Perrin can take you White Reed."

Perrin's head snapped around.

"I can?"

Teren said, "Graft house starts second ring tomorrow."

"And if cart back late?"

"Then I pay missed half."

Perrin looked suspicious.

"You hate paying missed half."

"I hate dry channels more."

There.

Short segment guide.

Not party.

Perrin could show maintained farm track to White Reed, then return for graft work if timing held.

"Does he know beyond White Reed?" I asked.

"To Sleeping Stone," Teren said.

Perrin said, "Barely. I was twelve."

"Then White Reed only."

Teren opened mouth.

I said, "You hired notes, not confidence theater."

He closed it.

Good.

Preparation.

Route sketch.

Old archive copy from Lakeward? Teren had hand copy.

Not map exactly.

Line with named markers, water branches, two old stone walls, Three Sisters contour scribble.

I compared to district archive notes copied yesterday.

Same sequence.

Different distances.

Teren's copy said White Reed to Sleeping Stone `one long climb`.

District archive said `approx. 3.4 road miles old measure`? Avoid modern miles? We have paces, road miles maybe prior. Better local distance uncertain. Use bells walking.

Teren: two bells when young.

Archive: no current time.

Fine.

I asked for physical landmarks.

White Reed: pale reed bed at channel fork.

Sleeping Stone: long dark slab over path, shaped like back under blanket.

Three Sisters: three narrow stone spires visible from lower hollow.

Mirror Spring: catch wall of black stone below white cliff seam.

Story names matched useful navigation.

Not magic.

Maybe.

Food:

flatbread.

dried fruit.

hard cheese.

smoked? Fine.

Three days modest.

Water flask.

Extra wrap.

Blanket roll.

No free expensive gear.

Teren offered old walking staff.

I looked at crutches.

"Inventory conflict."

He grunted.

Perrin laughed.

Sample bottle not yet.

Weather board at Morrow:

**RIDGE FOG MORNING / DRY DAY / EAST WIND LATE / NO RAIN WATCH**

Current only.

Three Sisters could differ.

Trial leg decision.

This mattered.

Crutches primary on unknown path.

Trial build could help on stable farm track and maybe free hands, but carrying extra weight plus unknown terrain.

Shop property.

Hark would murder me politely.

Already had been on boats.

Could leave at Morrow secured, but then if route includes stable sections I lose option.

Could carry wrapped, use only known dry stable stretches.

Weight cost.

I tested pack balance with it attached.

Manageable.

Not ideal.

Keep.

No wear today.

Skin rested.

Tomorrow maybe farm track only if dry.

Crutches on old path unless obvious stable ground.

Artifacts.

Line quietener.

Current reader.

Load tile.

Lot 67.

Did I need all?

I had been carrying them anyway.

Lot 67 could potentially compare timing if real interval question, but no reason yet.

Current reader maybe water/current direction? WS-F/9 slate current reader perhaps could be useful with flowing water, but limitations. Don't assume without state detail. Carry, characterize only if appropriate.

Load tile not obviously relevant.

Still carried.

No new purchase.

No money.

Magic.

Could test before trip.

No.

Save attention.

Protocol stayed 59 / 53 / 138.

Late afternoon Perrin took me lower channel.

Public cooperative section.

Chalk board nailed under roof.

Three readings across day.

Numbers meant local gauge marks, not flow volume.

Morning 6.2.

Midday 5.8.

Late 5.5.

Declining.

One day only.

Not trend beyond day.

Upper branch board? Different station, not visible.

"See?" Perrin said.

"I see this gauge declined today."

"You know what I mean."

"Yes. That's why I'm saying exact sentence."

He kicked dirt.

"You're irritating."

"Professionally now."

"Grandfather likes you."

"That's concerning."

"He doesn't."

"Better."

We walked rows.

Lower trees showed stress subtly.

Some leaves curled.

Fruit smaller? I couldn't know baseline.

Perrin knew.

He pointed Row Four.

"Those should be heavier by now."

"Could be water?"

"Could be heat. Could be root issue. Could be because this year's set was stupidly dense and Mom refused thinning enough because last year hail took half."

There.

Messy agriculture.

"So even source result won't explain fruit."

"No."

"Good."

He looked offended.

"Not good good. Evidence good."

"You talk like clerk."

"I've been paid as several."

At row end, older woman stood by gate.

Perrin's mother.

**Sera Sol**.

She had pruning knife and expression of person already informed about me and unconvinced.

"You're the walker."

"Apparently."

She looked at missing lower leg, crutches, pack.

Did not hide assessment.

"Teren sent a one-legged stranger up an abandoned path because he's too stubborn to wait for district."

"I negotiated."

"That doesn't improve sentence."

Fair.

Perrin said, "Mom."

"What? It's accurate."

I liked her more than Teren.

"Do you want me not to go?" I asked.

She answered too quickly.

"I want water."

Then slower:

"I want nobody hurt because my father thinks old stories are maps."

"Archive says places are real."

"Places being real doesn't make path safe."

"Agreed."

"If Three Sisters is bad, turn around."

"Contract says that."

"Contract is my father's handwriting with a clerk making it respectable. I'm telling you as person whose son will blame himself if you break your neck after he brought you here."

Perrin: "I wouldn't."

She looked at him.

"You absolutely would."

He shut up.

There.

Quest had people now.

Not just objective.

"I'll turn if route is beyond me," I said.

Sera nodded.

"And if spring is running strong?"

"I record that."

"Even if it means upper gates?"

"It means source appears strong at observation point. Upper gates would be separate claim."

She closed eyes briefly.

"Gods, my father hired a sentence."

"Twelve copper if sentence comes back with bottle."

She almost smiled.

Almost.

Then said, "Come eat. If you're walking tomorrow, I'm not letting Teren's travel ration be your dinner."

Food hospitality.

Not equipment windfall.

I accepted.

Family table.

Perrin's sisters **Lio** and **Mina** asked whether crutches made uphill harder.

"Yes."

"How much?"

"Depends hill."

"That's not number."

"Correct."

Mina asked if I was actually called Peg-Leg Greg.

Perrin had told them.

"No."

"But people call you that."

"Unfortunately."

"Where's peg?"

"Excellent question."

Sera looked at Perrin.

Perrin became fascinated by bread.

Teren arrived late.

He and Sera barely spoke about water.

That told me they had spoken too much already.

After dinner Teren brought small black pebble.

Not magical-looking.

Smooth.

"From Mirror Spring?" I asked.

"My father said."

"You know?"

"No."

Good.

He put it on table.

"I used to carry it when I walked route."

"Want me to take it?"

He hesitated.

"No."

Better.

"Why show me?"

"So you understand I'm not asking because of a children's story."

"You're asking because story is how your family remembers a route."

"And because route is how we remembered water didn't start at our gate."

There.

That was it.

Not sacred relic.

Not quest token.

Memory object.

He took pebble back.

"Bring your own rock if you need one."

I touched Tavi's striped rock in pack.

"Already overstocked."

Teren didn't understand.

Fine.

I slept in packing shed loft.

Employer lodging.

No copper.

Reasonable as hired field worker, not protagonist gift.

Cash twelve.

Ten floor.

Twenty-three Vale.

Tomorrow district runner brings bottle first ring.

Perrin takes me to White Reed.

Then turns back.

After White Reed, old path.

Sleeping Stone.

Three Sisters.

Mirror Spring if passable.

Return.

Three days food.

Twelve copper if bottle valid.

Eight if source reached without valid sample.

Four if Three Sisters proves unsafe and notes useful.

Zero guaranteed if I turn earlier except reimbursed fare and supplied food used in good faith.

That felt fair enough to be dangerous.

I wrote home note.

Longer than usual.

**Lakeward east, then Morrow Orchard. I took a short field contract. Lower orchard channels are running low. Old local story preserves a real route through White Reed, Sleeping Stone, Three Sisters Hollow, to Mirror Spring. District confirms places/source exist but old path is unmaintained and landslide affected Three Sisters. I'm being paid to return route/water observations and, if possible, a sealed supplemental spring sample. This does not make me district authority and sample will not prove cause by itself. Three days food supplied. Perrin Sol takes me only to White Reed, then returns to work. Cash 12c, Vale 23c. Ten floor intact. Trial build healthy. - Greg**

Then I added:

**This is an actual adventure now, which was more charming when theoretical.**

Postage from Morrow? Could go with morning cart. Bits.

I left note with packing clerk for Lakeward post run.

At loft, I laid gear out.

Crutches.

Pack.

Blanket.

Food.

Water.

Trial limb wrapped.

Notebook.

Artifacts.

Empty place for district bottle.

No sword suddenly appeared because chapter had become quest.

Old me found that funny.

Old me also knew most quests began with worse preparation than people admitted later.

Contractor.

That was what I was being.

Not hero.

Not chosen.

Not even sure path existed in useful form.

Somebody had a problem.

I had agreed to walk toward its source.

Tomorrow, finally, the road stopped being transportation.

It became the thing I had to survive.
# CHAPTER 460

## THE TRAILBLAZER

The bottle arrived before breakfast.

Adventure had paperwork.

Good.

The district runner set a padded wooden case on Morrow packing-shed table and made me read the seal form back to her.

Collector.

Route.

Fill point.

Observed conditions.

Witness if available.

Seal number before fill.

Seal number after fill.

Do not rinse bottle in source.

Do not touch inside neck or stopper.

Do not fill from standing pool if flowing source can be reached safely.

Do not alter source to obtain sample.

That last one mattered.

I signed receipt.

The Morrow cooperative had posted the one-copper bottle deposit already.

No money moved from me.

Cash twelve.

Vale twenty-three.

Protocol fifty-nine, fifty-three, one-thirty-eight.

Still boring.

Excellent.

The runner left.

Garrick Sol inspected the case like he expected bureaucracy to have hidden a second bottle inside out of spite.

"That's all?"

"Bottle, seal, form."

"They used to send a reader."

"They still are. Later."

"Later is useful word when your trees aren't thirsty."

Helena Sol was tying my food roll at the other end of table.

"Do not start before he leaves."

Garrick looked at her.

"I said one sentence."

"It was the first stair."

Jonah Sol came in carrying two water flasks.

That name was new.

Better.

I had spent part of last night looking at the names in my own notes and realizing the road had developed a disease.

Perrin.

Sera.

Lio.

Rusk.

Names I had already heard elsewhere, or names close enough to old ones that my notebook was starting to look like one family had colonized the continent.

So I fixed the notes before they hardened.

Jonah Sol.

Garrick Sol.

Helena Sol.

Ada and June.

Celia Brohm at Lakeward water office.

People deserved names that did not sound like I had drawn them from the same small sack of syllables.

Jonah put one flask beside my pack.

"Mine. You give it back at White Reed."

"Planning to."

"Grandfather says keeper has water."

"Grandfather says many things."

From table, Garrick said, "I can hear you."

"Good."

Helena smiled into knot.

We left after first ring.

Jonah carried his own small day bag.

I carried contract gear.

Crutches primary.

Trial limb wrapped against side of pack.

I had considered wearing it on maintained farm track.

Then looked at morning fog, damp stone, and several hours of unknown effort ahead.

No.

Save it.

The first stretch out of Morrow barely felt like quest.

Orchard rows.

Gate boxes.

Workers.

Cart ruts.

Low walls.

People called to Jonah by name.

Nobody called to me.

Good.

Water channel followed road uphill.

At Morrow it had been thin.

Above first terrace it was wider.

Not dramatically.

Enough to notice.

"Upper gate?" I asked.

Jonah pointed ahead.

"Shared split. Morrow branch takes left. Halden road takes right."

"Do we cross it?"

"Yes."

At split, wooden gates stood in stone throat.

Both open partially.

A chalk board under little roof showed morning marks.

I copied them.

Did not interpret.

Jonah watched.

"You could just say there's more water here."

"There is more water here."

"See?"

"That does not tell us why less reaches Morrow."

"I know."

"Then why are we fighting?"

"Because you make every sentence wear boots."

I liked that.

"Useful on trail."

"Terrible at dinner."

We kept climbing.

Maintained road narrowed after last packing yard.

Orchards broke into patches.

Stone walls older.

Some trees abandoned or feral.

Fruit small and hard.

Fog burned away slowly.

East wind had not started.

At a bend Jonah stopped.

"White Reed from here."

I saw pale stripe below us.

Not white exactly.

Silver-yellow reeds packed along shallow basin where two channels met.

A squat keeper house sat above ford.

Beyond it, road continued east as cart track.

Old path did not.

Old path climbed north beside reed basin and vanished into trees.

There.

Line between transport and adventure.

Of course there was a house at it.

Civilization liked putting paperwork at thresholds.

Keeper was **Mabel Crowe**.

Sixties maybe.

Short gray braid.

Mud boots.

One sleeve rolled higher than other because right forearm was wrapped in old burn scar.

She looked at Jonah.

"Garrick finally bullied somebody into walking it?"

"Contracted," I said.

She looked at me.

Then crutches.

Then pack.

"Worse."

Jonah said, "Morning, Mabel."

"You going too?"

"Only here."

"Good. Your mother has sense."

"That isn't why."

"Still good."

Different voice.

No dry-comeback academy. She spoke like conclusions had been waiting before we arrived.

I showed contract and district bottle receipt.

Mabel read slowly.

Twice.

"They put Three Sisters failure pay in writing."

"I insisted."

"Smart. Garrick would've paid you in regret."

Jonah said, "He's my grandfather."

"Then you know."

Maybe one dry line. Fine.

Mabel handed papers back.

"Ford first. Then you can decide whether old path deserves your remaining leg."

"Missing one already."

She stared.

"Yes. I counted."

Fair.

White Reed ford was not ankle deep.

Not knee either.

Mid-shin on Jonah.

Current modest but visible.

Bottom rounded stone with green film.

Bad crutch surface.

Old path crossed directly through it.

New keeper footbridge stood thirty paces downstream.

Narrow timber.

Rail one side.

"Why would I ford?" I asked.

Mabel pointed at route copy.

"Because old path did."

"Why would I care?"

Jonah laughed.

Mabel did not.

Then she smiled slightly.

"Good. Use bridge."

There.

Story route was not commandment.

The place mattered.

The exact historical foot placement did not.

I inspected bridge.

Dry enough.

Boards intact.

One-sided rail meant crutches still workable.

No trial limb.

Crossed slowly.

Fine.

On far side I went back toward ford bank without entering water.

White Reed soil.

Story said wet even when channel dry.

Current channel was not dry.

So story condition did not reproduce.

Still, something interesting.

Reed basin held water higher than incoming visible side channel suggested.

Could be groundwater.

Could be backwater geometry.

Could be seep.

Could be me not understanding basin.

Mabel crouched and pushed thin marked rod into mud near reed edge.

"You measuring?"

"Every morning."

"What?"

"Mud-water line in three holes. Not official. Mine."

"Why?"

She gave me look like question silly.

"Because reeds tell you after they're unhappy. Holes tell me before."

Good.

"Trend?"

"Lower than last week. Higher than channel makes people think."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning exactly that. Don't make me your clerk."

I wrote:

**White Reed: visible channel low relative to keeper expectation; shallow basin substrate remains wet. Keeper Mabel Crowe tracks three informal mud-water holes daily; says lower than last week, still higher than channel appearance suggests. No causal claim.**

Jonah read over shoulder.

"Boots."

"Excellent boots."

Mabel said, "Story people always liked this place because water hides here."

"Hides?"

"Not magic. Ground's full of old gravel under mud. Water moves sideways. My father called it hiding because he was better with children than geology."

That was exactly what I wanted.

Story language preserving observation without being technical report.

"Does White Reed feed Morrow?"

"Some years. Some ways. Ask district if you want percentages they don't have."

"Does Mirror Spring feed this basin?"

"Partly. Probably. There are side seeps. Rain shelf. Fog drip. Old stone channels nobody maps because half collapsed before my mother was born."

Messier.

Better.

"So strong Mirror sample doesn't prove strong Morrow supply."

"Of course not."

Jonah sighed.

"Can anybody in this district answer one thing with one thing?"

Mabel looked at him.

"Water doesn't."

That landed.

We ate early bread outside keeper house.

Jonah had to turn back soon if he wanted graft house by second ring plus lateness margin.

He kept looking at old path.

"I remember Sleeping Stone," he said.

"You were twelve."

"I know."

"You don't have to prove you remember."

"I know."

He sounded like he did not know emotionally.

Mabel cleaned mud rod.

"Your grandfather took you once."

"Twice."

"Second time you cried because thorn beetle got in your shirt."

"I was twelve."

"You said that already."

Jonah looked at me.

"I could take you farther."

There.

Temptation.

Local memory.

Extra body.

Company.

And his actual life waiting downhill.

"No."

"Sleeping Stone is only maybe two bells."

"Maybe."

"I know first climb."

"You have work."

"Grandfather said he'd cover half."

"If White Reed runs long. Not if you convert yourself into expedition staff."

"That's not your decision."

True.

I stopped.

"No. It's yours."

He looked surprised.

Good correction.

"My contract does not require you. Your family needs you. Your placement matters. If you decide to come anyway, I'm not going to pretend I own you. But I am not asking."

He stared up path.

Long time.

"Mom will be furious."

"Relevant."

"Grandfather will be pleased."

"Suspiciously relevant."

"Graft master will dock me."

"Very relevant."

He kicked pale reed stalk.

Mabel said, "Don't kick my reeds because adulthood is disappointing."

Jonah stopped.

Then laughed despite himself.

"I'm going back."

"Good," Mabel said.

He frowned at her.

"You could let me feel noble for one second."

"No."

He gave me his route memory anyway.

After White Reed, stay uphill of old stone channel until split oak.

At split oak, left path goes abandoned charcoal cut.

Right follows dark slab ridge.

Sleeping Stone visible only after last turn.

There was once a marker pile at split.

Maybe gone.

"If you hit two burned stumps, wrong way," Jonah said.

"How old are those instructions?"

"Nine years."

"Wonderful."

"The stumps were already old."

"Improving rapidly."

Mabel added current information.

"Split oak still standing last spring. Charcoal cut washed deeper. Don't take it. I haven't walked beyond first rise this year."

Current enough.

I copied separately:

**Jonah memory, age 12 / nine years old: uphill of stone channel; split oak; right toward slab ridge; old marker pile uncertain; burned stumps indicate charcoal cut/wrong route.**

**Mabel current-ish: split oak standing last spring; charcoal cut more washed; first rise only this year; no condition knowledge beyond.**

Different evidence ages.

Good.

Jonah handed me his flask.

"Keep it."

"You said return at White Reed."

"Mabel has water."

"You need one going back."

"I can fill here."

Mabel said, "He can. Take flask."

Useful ordinary loan.

Not magical gear.

"I'll return it."

Jonah shrugged.

"If you don't, Grandfather will add it to contract somehow."

Then he left.

Actually left.

Downhill.

No dramatic turn at path.

No last-minute party formation.

Within five minutes orchard trees swallowed him.

Mabel watched me watching.

"You nervous?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Everybody here likes that answer."

"People who say no before old road are either lying or young."

"I have been both."

She pointed at pack.

"Too heavy?"

"Manageable."

"That's not answer."

Apparently disease spread.

I adjusted shoulder strap.

"Heavy enough uphill will matter. Not heavy enough to leave required gear."

"Better."

I checked crutch tips.

Wrap.

Straps.

Water.

Bottle case secure high in pack.

Trial limb wrapped.

Weather.

Fog mostly lifted.

East wind beginning in reed tops.

Dry forecast still.

Old path entrance was narrow dirt line above basin.

First twenty paces easy.

Then roots.

Then slope.

I stopped after maybe fifty.

Looked back.

Mabel keeper house below.

White Reed silver around water.

Maintained bridge.

Farm road.

Orchards beyond.

Could still turn around and lose nothing but dignity, which had never been expensive.

I continued.

The first rise was harder than map implied.

Maps rarely included shoulders.

Crutches bit dirt well where dry.

Roots created step problems.

I used old technique.

Not magic.

Not S-class anything.

Three points.

Set.

Move.

Breathe before needed.

Don't wait for fatigue to announce itself.

Rest on schedule rather than pride.

Pack changed balance backward.

I shortened stride.

At one steep patch I sat and scooted three body lengths rather than pretend standing method superior.

Adventure dignity remained cheap.

At top of first rise, Mabel was no longer visible.

Only reed basin through branches.

Isolation arrived quietly.

No music.

No monster.

Just nobody close enough to hear normal voice.

I sat on flat stone and drank.

Heart working.

Arms warm.

Right shoulder fine.

Left residual limb fine because no socket.

Crutch palms beginning pressure but normal.

Good.

Old stone channel appeared beside path.

Half buried.

Not carrying surface water.

Moss inside.

Damp at bottom.

Story path and water path overlapping again.

I did not assume connection to Mirror.

I wrote.

Then heard stone click uphill.

One click.

Pause.

Another.

Not falling continuously.

Movement.

I froze.

Old me came closer.

Not locked-in fully.

Just attention changing shape.

Wind east.

Leaves moving right-to-left.

Click came against wind side.

Something stepping.

Could be person.

Could be animal.

I moved off center of path to wider patch beside channel wall.

Back protected by stone enough.

Crutches planted.

No stupid weapon improvisation.

Wait.

A long-bodied animal came through brush uphill.

Not monster.

Deer-sized maybe smaller.

Six legs.

Gray-brown hide.

Flat antler-like plates sweeping backward from skull.

It stopped when it saw me.

I stopped harder.

We regarded each other.

I knew broad category from first life.

Shelf grazer.

Not exact local species.

Usually flight animal.

Usually mattered.

Its left rear leg was caught in trailing vine? No. Thin old wire.

Ah.

Old route infrastructure again.

Wire loop dragged from leg into brush.

Animal shifted.

Wire tightened.

It jerked.

Bad.

I was not touching that.

Could maybe cut wire if animal restrained.

Animal was not restrained in useful sense.

It had six legs and several opinions.

I backed one crutch-length.

Slow.

Grazer lowered head.

Plates forward enough to make geometry obvious.

Not attack yet.

Pressure.

I gave path.

More space downhill.

Animal pulled uphill.

Wire caught branch.

It panicked.

Now action.

It lunged sideways, not at me exactly, but path was narrow and I occupied part of available world.

Old me calculated before current body finished objecting.

Do not retreat straight downhill on crutches.

Drop center.

I sat hard behind channel wall.

Not graceful.

Grazer crossed where chest had been, plates clipping leaves.

Wire snapped branch.

Animal stumbled, recovered on too many legs, dragged loose wire uphill, disappeared.

Silence.

My heart upgraded contract price without authorization.

I stayed seated.

Count.

Hands.

Elbows.

Hip.

Residual limb.

Pack.

Bottle.

All fine.

One crutch had fallen across path.

Retrieved from seated position.

No chase.

No rescue attempt.

No magic.

I inspected where wire had caught.

Old copper line, green-black with age, partly buried along channel wall.

Maybe old signal? Water marker? Fence? Unknown.

Animal had pulled several lengths free.

I did not follow.

I marked hazard:

**First rise above White Reed: old thin wire exposed along path/channel edge, partly buried, now pulled loose by local six-legged shelf grazer. Entanglement hazard. Animal departed uphill with some wire trailing. Do not assume wire function.**

Useful route note.

Also:

**Path narrow enough animal passage required yielding. Wider refuge at channel-wall break approx. first rise.**

That was adventure.

Not glorious.

I preferred glorious in retrospect anyway.

I waited another few minutes.

Then stood carefully.

The path continued uphill toward split oak.

Sleeping Stone somewhere beyond.

White Reed no longer visible.

Jonah already headed back to work.

Mabel below keeping water holes.

Garrick waiting for evidence.

Helena waiting for me not to be stupid.

Twelve copper waiting at theoretical successful end.

And somewhere above, water had gone somewhere.

I adjusted pack.

Set crutches.

Continued.

Trailblazer was generous title.

The trail already existed.

Mostly.

My job was to find out how much of it still did.
